sup-a4df133b477018fb-w1:a.hint: Mark the centre of the circle. Which components of the real forces point towards it?
notes: Use ΣF_radial = mv²/r towards the centre. “Centripetal force” names this resultant; it is not an additional force.
At the top and bottom of a vertical circle the weight contributes with different radial signs. At loss of contact or a just-taut string, set the contact force or tension to zero.

sup-a4df133b477018fb-w1:b.hint: Draw a force equation for each connected body, using compatible positive directions along the string.
notes: An inextensible taut string links the accelerations. A light string over an ideal pulley has the same tension on both sides.
To find acceleration, combine the equations to eliminate internal tension. Then substitute back into a single-body equation to find the tension.

sup-a4df133b477018fb-w1:c.i.hint: Choose the object or system and identify the resultant force, rather than using one force on its own.
notes: Newton’s second law is ΣF = ma. Resolve into independent directions; zero acceleration requires zero resultant force in that direction.
Newton’s third-law forces act on different bodies and are the same kind of interaction. Balanced forces act on the same body.

sup-a4df133b477018fb-w1:c.iii.hint: Use the rotational counterparts of force, mass and acceleration. Is the torque constant?
notes: Use net torque τ = Iα. With constant angular acceleration, ω = ω₀ + αt and θ = ω₀t + ½αt².
Use radians and the moment of inertia about the stated axis. Moment of inertia depends on how mass is distributed, not only the total mass.

sup-a4df133b477018fb-w1:d.hint: The spring force changes as the spring stretches. How is that represented on a force–extension graph?
notes: For a Hooke’s-law spring, F = kx and elastic energy = ½kx². Here x is extension or compression from the natural length.
When spring, kinetic and gravitational energy all change, include all three stores. Do not use F_final x for the spring’s work.

sup-a4df133b477018fb-w1:e.hint: Compare the initial and final energy stores. Which transfers occur between those two states?
notes: Use E_k = ½mv² and near-surface ΔE_p = mgΔh. Work by a constant force is W = Fs cos θ, using the angle between force and displacement.
The work–energy theorem uses the net work. With friction, include the energy dissipated rather than assuming mechanical energy is conserved.

sup-a4df133b477018fb-w1:f.i.hint: Isolate the named object. Add an arrow for each interaction it has with its surroundings.
notes: Draw only forces acting on this object: weight, contact force, tension, friction or other stated interactions. Label directions and place weight at the centre of mass.
The resultant is the vector sum of these forces. Do not add an extra “ma force” or put a Newton’s-third-law reaction on the same object.

notes: When external impulse is negligible, Σmu = Σmv. Keep velocity signs, and apply the equation separately in each direction for a two-dimensional collision.
